group.passage:
Yawning is a universal human behavior, yet its contagious nature remains a fascinating mystery to scientists. Simply seeing someone yawn—or even just thinking about it—can trigger the same response in ourselves, a phenomenon known as contagious yawning. [[1]]
A widely accepted explanation highlights the role of mirror neurons, specialized brain cells that activate not only when we act but also when we observe the same action performed by others. [[2]] This automatic imitation appears to serve a deeper purpose: helping us understand and respond appropriately to others’ emotional states, which in turn strengthens social bonding.
Advancements in brain imaging, particularly functional MRI, have offered further evidence supporting this theory. [[3]] These areas are associated with recognizing emotions and planning social responses, suggesting that mirror neurons may provide a neural foundation for empathy.
Interestingly, not everyone is equally affected by contagious yawning, and this variability may reveal important clues about how empathy develops. Studies show that children under five rarely “catch” yawns from others, likely because their mirror neural system, critical for empathy, is still developing. [[4]] These findings suggest a strong link between contagious yawning and empathy, which develops gradually in childhood and varies across individuals. Some researchers thus conclude that susceptibility to contagious yawning may serve as an indicator of mirror neuron function and empathetic capacity.

options_bank.A: Similarly, people with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) tend to show reduced yawn contagion.
options_bank.B: Studies have found that children respond more strongly to yawns from close companions than to those from strangers.
options_bank.C: When we witness someone yawn, these neurons trigger similar neural patterns in our brain, prompting us to mimic the behavior unconsciously.
options_bank.D: Brain scans show that observing a yawn activates brain regions involved in emotional processing, such as the anterior cingulate cortex and the right inferior frontal gyrus.
options_bank.E: Although it may seem like a simple reflex, researchers believe this behavior reveals important insights into how our brains are wired for social connection and even empathy.
